storm.summary_layperson: It's a clear, calm evening on tap for the cove — no storm activity anywhere nearby and nothing in the models suggests that changing before 10 PM.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air is actually running about 3–4°F cooler than the 70°F Sound water right now, so there's no marine-layer buffer in play tonight — though it doesn't matter, since there's no storm activity for it to blunt anyway.
storm.detail_html:
Instability is essentially nonexistent this evening — CAPE is sitting at just 10 J/kg at the current hour and drops to 0 J/kg by 6 PM in the HRRR run. KOKX radar shows no echoes anywhere in range, and there are no active NWS watches, warnings, or advisories for the area.

The Sound's usual protective trick — cool water creating a stable marine layer that chokes off approaching storms — isn't set up the way it normally is. Water is 69.8°F and air is only 66.2°F, so the air is actually colder than the water rather than warmer, meaning there's no meaningful stable layer to speak of. That's the opposite of the setup that usually helps the cove, but with nothing on radar and no CAPE to work with, it's a moot point tonight.

The most likely outcome for the 5–9 PM window is a dry, quiet evening with clear-to-partly-cloudy skies, both at the cove and in the surrounding towns — there's no local reason to expect anything different here than inland.

What would change this call: a fast-developing pop-up cell riding in on the shear (0–6 km shear is a respectable 19–21 kt out of the WSW) or a frontal passage that brings real CAPE back into the picture. Neither is signaled by the current HRRR run through 7 PM, and the forecast hours beyond that aren't available from this model cycle, so this call should be treated as most reliable through about 7 PM and reasonably stable beyond that given the lack of any destabilizing trend.

wind.tactics_blurb: There's no thermal sea breeze tonight — air is actually running cooler than the Sound, so this is a straight gradient-wind evening in the 8–12 kt range, gradually backing toward NNE and easing after sunset. Current Riverside YC readings are running more easterly than the model's NE call, so start mid-line and watch for the breeze to swing right toward the forecast direction as the evening settles in.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-wind evening, not a sea-breeze day: the air–water temperature difference (deltaT) is actually -3.6°F — the air over land is running colder than the 69.8°F Sound water — which is the reverse of the setup a thermal sea breeze needs. Zero percent of coastal stations are reading southerly, confirming there's no sea-breeze circulation trying to establish itself. The breeze filling the course tonight is straight synoptic gradient flow out of the NE-quadrant.

Without a thermal engine driving the wind, there isn't a strong geography-based favored side the way there is on a classic sea-breeze afternoon — pressure should stay reasonably even across the course, so we're calling this one center-favored rather than committing hard to a shore.

Worth flagging: the HRRR model is forecasting NE (42–50°) through the window, but the live reading at Riverside YC right now is out of the E (90°) at 11.2 kt gusting 20.5 kt, and the broader western-Sound station group is averaging ESE (113°) — a 50–70° divergence from the model. Because this isn't a thermal sea-breeze regime, the maturation-correction framework doesn't apply here, so we're going with the model call for the forecast table, but sailors on the water should expect the breeze may run more easterly than shown, especially early in the window, with a likely veer back toward the model's NE direction as the evening progresses.

Speed-wise, 8–12 kt with gusts into the high teens/low 20s is comfortable full-sail breeze for most one-designs — enough to sail well but not overpowering. Shift character is a slow, continuous backing trend (NE swinging toward NNE) rather than sharp oscillations, so expect a gradually persistent shift through the beat rather than a shifty, puffy track.

Data note: HRRR hourly output was only available through 7 PM this cycle (fh1–fh4); the 8–10 PM hours above are extrapolated from that trend — continued gradient flow, easing and backing gently as the boundary layer stabilizes after sunset — rather than a direct model pull.
